title: Preparing to Engineer an Instructional Innovation
author: Terry Yu
summary: Terry Yu offers a practical walkthrough of using a design-based research (DBR) conjecture map as a framework for planning instructional innovations in real classroom settings, illustrated through a dialogue with Claude Opus running a custom system prompt that guides educators through the process. The article is structured in three parts: an orientation explaining the tool, an example conversation showing the DBR consultant prompt in action with a middle school English project aimed at shifting students' epistemic self-perceptions, and the full system prompt educators can copy and use themselves. The central pedagogical problem is students in high-compliance urban schools who have internalized a fatalistic view of school -- 'it's a game of chance, effort doesn't matter' -- and who therefore need an encounter with their own agency rather than a lecture about it. Yu argues that the conjecture map is a rigorous enough tool to force teachers to specify exactly what they expect to happen and why, making tacit design assumptions explicit and testable before classroom implementation. The article is simultaneously a practical contribution (a usable system prompt) and a theoretical argument for treating instructional design as disciplined inquiry rather than intuitive craft.
points: * A conjecture map structures instructional design by making the causal chain explicit: what embodied tools and activity structures are you deploying, what mediating processes do you expect them to produce, and what outcomes do you predict will follow -- forcing teachers to articulate and test their implicit theories. * The student population's core belief -- 'school is a game of chance, I have little control over outcomes, so why invest effort?' -- is a correct reading of their actual environment rather than irrational pessimism; any effective intervention must address the actual causal dynamics rather than simply affirming student agency. * Yu's use of AI as a design-based research consultant (via system prompt) models how LLMs can serve as structured interlocutors for iterative professional thinking, with the AI pressing for specificity and pushing back on vague claims rather than simply affirming the educator's initial framing. * The system prompt methodology -- giving educators a replicable conversational structure they can run in any LLM -- distributes a sophisticated research-design scaffold to practitioners who would not otherwise have access to DBR expertise. * Involving LLMs as both a research tool and a student-facing learning tool within the same intervention design creates a second purpose: giving students a direct encounter with AI as an agency-amplifying resource rather than a knowledge oracle.
quotes: My name is Harry. I have two middle school English teachers who want to give it a try, and we're hoping to make an impact on how the kids understand their own agency as learners. It's tough because they're in an urban school with a strong compliance ethic so my participating teachers are working against the grain.

This post isn't an essay. Instead, I'm providing you with a system prompt you can read through, copy and paste it into an LLM, and try out on your own. System prompts tune an LLM to perform a long conversation with considerable nuance even as the chat develops along a solid structure.
I'm working as a design-based research consultant today -- here to help you articulate a conjecture map for something you're designing that will live in a real setting of practice.
